newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Coup allegations expose Kremlin power battle.
newsitem.headline: Coup allegations expose Kremlin power battle.

text.p: The power battle smouldering inside the Kremlin burst into flames on Wednesday when Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused security chief and main rival Alexander Lebed of plotting to seize power.
"(Lebed) has decided to move ahead using force instead of waiting for the next presidential poll," said Kulikov, effectively declaring war on the outspoken Lebed.

"He said he would become president before the end of the incumbent president's tenure. It is clear that this can be achieved only by unconstitutional means, by means of mutiny," he told a news conference.
It was an extraordinary personal attack, even by the anarchic standards of modern Russian politics, and Lebed was quick to respond.
"There can be no talk of a mutiny," Lebed told Interfax news agency. Asked to explain Kulikov's charges, Lebed replied sarcastically: "The poor thing has got everything wrong."
Lebed, Kulikov and other top officials are locked in a power struggle which has worsened since President Boris Yeltsin announced on September 5 that he planned to have heart surgery.

The conflict between the two men escalated just one day after Yeltsin told his subordinates to stop their "verbal duels", which have mainly swirled around the peace deal Lebed signed in late August to end the 21-month Chechen war.

Kulikov's attack seemed to be a straightforward attempt to rid the Kremlin of a man who has made many enemies since being named to his post in late June, especially through his criticism of how the Chechen campaign was conducted.
In August, Lebed said Kulikov was mainly to blame for the Chechen fiasco and asked Yeltsin to choose between the two men. But Yeltsin told Lebed to knuckle down and stop complaining.
Rumours of plots and potential coups d'etats are all too frequent in Russia, alarming nervous financial markets abroad.

Tanks have appeared in Moscow twice in just over five years, once in August 1991 when hardliners tried to oust Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and again in October 1993 when Russian President Boris Yeltsin tried to oust a new batch of hardliners holed up in the White House government building.

RIA news agency, usually close to the Kremlin, said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had summoned intelligence chiefs and Russia's defence and interior ministers to a special meeting on Thursday. It was not clear whether Lebed would attend.

Kulikov alleged that Lebed had been promised 1,500 Chechen gunmen to help him take power in Moscow and later told Russian television that security would be increased in big cities to fend off possible Chechen attacks.

"We have information that he is planning to go on vacation soon to prepare to use force on a local level," Kulikov told the news conference, adding that he had passed all details of the Lebed's activities to Chernomyrdin.
He also accused Lebed of planning to set up an elite legion to combat civil unrest and said the security chief was setting up his own power structures.

But Lebed said it was no secret he had asked the interior and defence ministries to set up a single brigade of 3,000 to 3,500 people in each region to ensure "there would be some kind of power in the state".
He said the two ministries had told him they could do so by the end of 1999.
